title: Jet Fuel Hits a Record Price, and Holiday Plane Tickets Are Soaring
summary:
Planning to fly somewhere for the holidays? Get ready to pay more — maybe a lot more.

The big reason is jet fuel, the special fuel airplanes burn, and one of the airline industry's biggest expenses. The average price of jet fuel in the United States reached $4.90 a gallon on Thursday, according to the tracking firm Argus. That is the highest single-day average the firm has ever recorded, and more than twice the price a year ago.

Airlines are passing part of that cost on to passengers. "Airfares right now are at what we see as a 10-year high because of the high cost of jet fuel," said Hayley Berg, the lead economist at Hopper, a travel tech company. According to Berg, Thanksgiving airfares are up about 30% compared with last year, and tickets for the Christmas holiday are up more than 20%.

Even so, travelers keep booking. Delta Air Lines CEO Ed Bastian said customers have shown a "limited amount of resistance" and still view airfare as "reasonably affordable." Chris Sununu, head of the trade group Airlines for America, said the airlines themselves are absorbing most of the extra fuel cost, but some of it "unfortunately has to be passed on to the customer."

People are adapting in different ways. Many booked their holiday trips earlier than usual this year, hoping to lock in prices before they rose. Others are skipping the plane entirely. Rachel Stern of Frederick, Maryland, said tickets for her and her kids cost too much, so she plans to drive to Chicago instead.

Some industry leaders think fares could climb further next year, especially in Europe. The picture may be slightly better in the United States, which has more oil-producing and refining capacity than Europe.
why_it_matters: Millions of families fly to visit relatives over Thanksgiving and Christmas, so higher fares hit household budgets directly. The story also shows how the price of one fuel can ripple through the whole travel industry.

background_read: Jet fuel is the special fuel that airplane engines burn, and it is one of the biggest costs an airline has.

When fuel prices rise, airlines often pass part of the extra cost on to passengers through higher ticket prices, especially at busy holiday times like Thanksgiving and Christmas, when many people want to fly.
Tracking firms and travel companies watch fuel prices and fares closely and report how they change compared with earlier years.
The United States produces and refines a great deal of its own oil, which can soften the effect of fuel price rises compared with places that import more.
